articles.title: The rise of hairy young women: ‘I know people who dye their armpit hair, so it stands out more’
articles.summary: When Phoebe Bridgers appeared at Venice international film festival with unshaven legs this weekend, it shouldn’t have made headlines – but did. What do young women make of the current expectations around depilation? In 2026, female body hair feels as if it should be the least of anyone’s concerns.
body: Even so, her au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations. Vogue decreed that “rather than undermining the femininity of the look, unapologetic hair sharpened it”, and pictures of the 32-year-old’s hair-covered calves were generally praised by fans. But what do other gen Z and millennial women make of the decision to ditch the razor?

“Hell yeah!” is 27-year-old PhD student Anna Busuttil’s response. “I think it’s awesome; cool and rebellious,” she says – a view that chimes with that of most of the women I speak to outside University College London’s Bloomsbury campus. Busuttil says she sees a lot more women nowadays choosing not to remove their body hair. “I know people who dye their armpit hair a certain colour as well, so it stands out even more. I feel like leg hair is more taboo for women; it feels like such a ‘masculine’ thing, and legs are supposed to be a really sexy part of a woman.”
points: What do young women make of the current expectations around depilation?
In 2026, female body hair feels as if it should be the least of anyone’s concerns.

articles.title: Jibby Beane obituary
articles.summary: My glamorous friend Jibby Beane, who has died aged 84, was known in London’s fashion and art worlds as an energetic and unique figure. Blessed with fabulous blond good looks, during the 1990s she appeared on the catwalk for Vivienne Westwood, was featured in countless style magazines and ran an art…
body: Wherever Jibby arrived, laced into a Westwood corset and tottering on platform shoes, everyone knew who she was. She had started modelling in the 60s and appeared in the first Andrex television commercial to feature a labrador retriever puppy in 1972. She had also worked for the couturier Victor Stiebel. In 1963 she married Kenneth Beane, whom she had known since childhood.

Talented at decorating houses, and selling them, she studied interior design and got a diploma from Richmond Adult College in the late 80s. She went on to establish her own company, Dream Designs, and worked occasionally at the Design and Decoration Building in Chelsea, where she was a greeter; there she met Westwood in the ladies’ loos. She had also met a young art student, Jonathan Goslan, in 1991, which led to her separation from Ken.

By 1992, Jibby was the face of Westwood’s Mayfair stores, holding court every Saturday as she slipped into one outfit after another. “She seemed to have multiple sides – from diva to comedian,” said Mark Garcia, a colleague. “But my favourite was the one she called ‘Mother Beane’. If you needed advice, or comfort, or reassurance, she would give it all. She was incredibly kind.”

articles.title: Alice Zaslavsky’s satay-butter charred cabbage wedges with fragrant chicken mince – recipe
articles.summary: The cookbook author has a shortcut method for blanching vegetables that saves on time, equipment and water. Check out more Alice Zaslavsky recipes. I love a burnt brassica, and there’s no better flavour than the big mama herself: the cabbage.
body: Vegetables in the cruciferous family, like brussels sprouts, broccoli and cauliflower, have naturally bitter compounds. However, with concentrated heat, this bitterness is transformed into sweetly caramelised corners and burnished bits.
It’s one way to make brassica boo-ers braver. But getting cooked-through cabbage with a softened heart and gnarly edges requires a delicate balance of time under heat.

Lucky for us, the sharp bitterness of cabbage has been bred out of more conventional styles on supermarket and greengrocer shelves. Modern varieties are much milder, sweeter and less fibrous, meaning they require far less cooking than the cabbages of old.
That’s why these days, I’m fond of a gentler method that softens their rawness without overcooking: the kettle-blanch.

articles.title: ‘As creamy as Haagen Dazs’: I tried three affordable ice-cream machines – the $24 beat them all
articles.summary: From the portable My Mug to the sleek Soft Serve Machine, I reviewed the Dash ice-cream makers worth your freezer space. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things. Soft serve always feels like a special occasion.
body: Naturally I’m thrilled to see soft serve has enjoyed a renaissance, especially in my city. Last year, cronut creator Dominique Ansel made waves with soft serve dipped in French butter. Soft serve margaritas took over TikTok this year. And if line culture is any indication of interest, soft serve spots like Culture and, in my neighborhood, Lisbonata, now draw round-the-block throngs of treat seekers.

Rather than spending hours (and a small fortune) waiting in line, I decided to see if I could spin up some decent soft serve in my own kitchen. But these machines, such as Ninja’s buzzy Creami Scoop and Swirl, can be pricey, and I couldn’t stomach the $349 cost for something we’d probably only end up using a few times a year (though the cult of Creami may argue it’s worth it ).

Enter Dash, a budget appliance brand known for its $11 mini waffle makers. I decided to try its line of ultra-affordable frozen dessert machines: the Soft Serve Ice Cream Maker, Deluxe Gelato & Ice Cream Maker and compact My Mug.

articles.title: 6 Steps to Glass Skin, According to K-Beauty Experts
articles.summary: Glass skin is rooted in K-beauty practices, imparting a dewy, almost reflective complexion. Here’s how to get the look, plus the products to shop.
body: With unprecedented accessibility—there’s no shortage of K-beauty-inspired skin-care products formulated to brighten, hydrate, and impart glowing skin ASAP—it’s easy for anyone to take up the approach. And while Choi points out that the glass-skin trend exploded in popularity due to social media, “ultimately becoming a global phenomenon,” the concept itself has ancient cultural ties. “South Koreans and skin care go back thousands of years to the time of the Three Kingdoms era (37–668 BC), when the ideology of beauty standards was coined young-yook-il-chi-sa-sang, meaning ‘within a beautiful body, rests a beautiful soul,’” board-certified dermatologist Christine Hall, MD explains.

There’s Gemini, a shimmering candy pink named for her star sign; Monaco, a terracotta nod to the place she calls home; Monet, an apricot shade inspired by her favorite artist. articles.title: On California's Central Coast, an Indoor-Outdoor Museum Connects Visitors With Centuries of Chumash Heritage
articles.summary: Inside the new Chumash Museum and Cultural Center in Santa Ynez, California.
body: The Chumash Heritage Marine Sanctuary was featured on Condé Nast Traveler' s Bright Ideas in Travel 2025. Read the full list of winners here.

I am greeted by cast iron doors, engraved with spiraling pictographs and cool to the touch, even in the morning heat of June. I grip the handle—shaped, I'll learn, like a clapper stick, a traditional Chumash percussion instrument—and push it open. The sounds of birdsong, layered and ambient, rise toward a curved ceiling where light moves like cloud shadow. Here, what lies indoors simulates the beauty of the natural world.

I have entered an 'Ap, the Chumash word for home, reimagined at monumental scale. The traditional version would have been made of willow branches and tule reeds, but this one is steel and stone with the same circular, embracing shape: This is the 14,000-square-foot Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center, which opened on May 15, 2025, after 20 years in the making. Every detail has been designed with intention by Native American architect Johnpaul Jones.

articles.title: Carlos Sainz Shares the “Fundamental” Grooming Tip Every “Gentleman” Should Know
articles.summary: The Formula 1 driver shares his favorite fragrances to spritz, some thoughts on the stigma surrounding male beauty, and a new skin treatment.
body: Carlos Sainz likes to get “tough” with his skincare. While sharing his Beauty Secrets with Vogue, the Formula 1 driver applies Augustinus Bader cleanser with noticeable vigor. “I like doing it hard; I don’t know why,” he says.

However, other aspects of the racecar driver’s routine are decidedly more gentle—gentle manly, that is. Before wrapping up his grooming routine, Sainz spritzes himself with his version of “aftershave.”

“I always believe in a gentleman smelling like a gentleman, always smelling good. And a good aftershave is always fundamental for that,” the 32-year-old says, while clutching a bottle of Acqua di Giò Profondo. The aromatic and aquatic eau de parfum isn’t the only fragrant part of Sainz’s morning wellness routine: he also lights Byredo’s Lost Road Candle, a citrus and black pepper-forward scent, to set the vibe. “Why not?” he asks. And why not, indeed.

“For men nowadays, there’s a stigma of grooming and taking care of yourself that maybe you don’t feel very comfortable with,” Sainz continues. “But I’ve realized that nowadays pretty much every man does it. Don’t be shy about it; share it! Remember to take care of yourself.”

articles.title: Inside the Most Glittering Parties of Venice Film Festival 2026 (So Far)
articles.summary: From fashion dinners to charity galas, here, find Vogue’s roundup of the best and most star-studded parties at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.
body: It’s September in Venice, which can only mean one thing: the annual film festival, widely regarded as one of the world’s most prestigious, has landed. But alongside the premieres on the Lido and the photo calls at the Hotel Excelsior dock, there’s an equally fundamental part of these celebrations of cinema taking place all over the city: the parties.

Whether it’s fashion and jewelry brand dinners, cocktails hosted by international awards bodies, or charity galas, the evenings at the festival are just as busy as the daytime screenings—and typically take place in one of the historic five-star hotels that dot the Grand Canal for a quintessentially Venetian backdrop.

articles.title: RF Kuang's New Novel Takes On the Angst of a Diaspora Kid on a Study-Abroad Trip to Taipei
articles.summary: The Taipei Story author on how home, identity, and diaspora kid woes inform her latest work.
body: From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of traveling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather—which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot—these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places.
Condé Nast Traveler recently spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and being split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is available in bookstores now.

The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan.
